newsitem.title: FRANCE: British Aerospace joins Lockheed fighter bid.
newsitem.headline: British Aerospace joins Lockheed fighter bid.

text.p: British Aerospace Plc announced at the Paris air show Wednesday that it was joining U.S. defence giant Lockheed Martin's bid for the Joint Strike Fighter programme, the next-generation U.S. fighter plane.

British Aerospace's decision ends months of speculation as to whether it would team up with Lockheed or rival Boeing Co. to bid to build up to 3,000 multi-role fighters for the U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, which all currently fly different aircraft.
The British navy is also buying the futuristic fighter.
"With a requirement for over 3,000 aircraft, JSF is the most significant transatlantic military programme of the 21st century," British Aerospace Chief Executive Sir Richard Evans said.

Evans said the decision could lead to wider collaboration, pointing out that British Aerospace also is bidding with Lockheed for the multi-billion dollar Anglo-U.S. Tracer competition to develop a new army reconnaissance vehicle.
"I want to see the relationship grow," he told a news conference. "We are living in a much a smaller world today, there are a lot of opportunities here and I think we just need to see what happens."
But he denied the move meant the company was turning its back on efforts to seek European industry mergers or would alienate its European partners on other aircraft projects.
"I am not anticipating any problems at all," he said.
A naval version of the Joint Strike Fighter will feature short take-off and landing capability to replace U.S. Marine and Royal Navy Harriers.
British Aerospace would be bring its expertise in vertical and short take-off and landing (VSTOL) technology as well as its lean production techniques to the Lockheed bid.

"We have been in the VSTOL and STOVL (short takeoff and vertical landing) business for a number of years," he said. "I think the decision for BAe is a decision that's completely understood across the European aerospace industrial base."

Evans also denied that Boeing had been rejected due to pressure from British Aerospace's partners in European plane-making consortium Airbus Industrie, which is opposing Boeing's proposed takeover of McDonnell Douglas.
McDonnell Douglas, which was British Aerospace's orginal running mate for the Joint Strike Fighter, decided to merge with Boeing after being dropped by the Pentagon from the competition in November.

Instead Boeing and Lockheed were selected to develop two government-funded prototypes apiece, with a view to picking the winning design in the year 2001 so that first aircraft go into service in 2008.

"Last November ... we had agreed that the first phone call I was to make after being told that Lockheed Martin had been selected was to British Aerospace and indeed we made that call," said Lockheed Chairman Norman Augustine.
The winner of the fighter competition stands to net a production contract worth over $100 billion alone for the U.S. requirement for up to 3,000 planes.

Mike Rouse, managing director of British Aerospace's military aircraft division, said British Aerospace hoped it could make sufficient contributions to the prototype work to earn a workshare of around 10 percent, which could be worth over $10 billion if Lockheed won the eventual production contract.

British Aerospace was assured of a place on one of the teams because Britain's Ministry of Defence has contributed 200 million British pounds ($327 million) to the development programme to find a replacement for its own navy's Sea Harriers.
